v.why: Without a direct input-to-output skip, a strong conv on the node2->output edge supplies much-needed capacity and gradient flow, while with a skip present it adds little (exps 7, 8 and 10 vs 1-5).
When node1 does not feed the output directly, the residual input->output path matters more (exp 19 vs 11 and 18).
Adding a residual where none existed helps more than swapping out an existing conv or pool for a skip (exps 11 and 17 vs 12 and 14).
Pruning the node1->output edge is more harmful when there is no input->output skip to compensate (exps 32 and 33 vs 31 and 35).
Replacing a 3x3 conv with parameter-free pooling loses capacity, unlike replacing none or skip (exp 51 vs 52-54).
Deleting the residual skip on the input->output edge typically hurts trainability more than deleting a conv there (exps 62 and 64-67).
Replacing a pooling op on the final edge with an identity removes harmful smoothing, giving larger gains than replacing a conv (exp 88 vs 82 and 83).
Adding a 1x1 conv on a missing node1->output edge adds capacity, whereas replacing a skip or 3x3 conv with it is neutral or harmful (exps 71 and 75-78 vs 72 and 79).
A conv on edge 1->2 is wasted when node1 receives no input because edge 0 is none (exp 41 vs 44).
Turning the final conv into a skip removes key capacity when there is no other direct route to the output (exp 81 vs 82 and 85).
